idiom_name: val + read-only collection interfaces + data class copy()
implementation_notes: Kotlin separates val (read-only binding) from var and its collection interfaces (List, Set, Map) expose no mutating methods, so a data class with val properties plus the generated copy() is the built-in wither and replaces the hand-written immutable type. Read-only is not immutable, however: a MutableList can be passed where List is expected and changed afterwards through the original reference, and the Kotlin documentation distinguishes the two explicitly, so data shared across modules or threads needs kotlinx.collections.immutable - persistentListOf/persistentMapOf, or the ImmutableList/ImmutableSet/ImmutableMap adapters - whose update methods return new persistent instances that share structure. The classic defensive-copy structure is still justified at Java interop boundaries, because collections coming from Java code may be mutable and mutated on the other side.
code_sketch:
data class Config(val name: String, val ports: List<Int>)
fun Config.withPort(port: Int) = copy(ports = ports + port)   // new instance, receiver untouched

val base = Config("api", listOf(8080))
val next = base.withPort(8443)

// true immutability + sharing: kotlinx.collections.immutable.persistentListOf(8080)
pitfalls: Read-only interfaces are not immutable: val list: List<Int> = mutableListOf(...) can still change under a reader through the MutableList alias.

data class copy() is shallow: nested mutable collections and arrays stay shared, and arrays also break the generated equals/hashCode with reference equality, so a data class with an array component is a broken key.
Collections returned from Java code arrive as platform types and may be mutable and mutated later, so copy defensively or use a persistent collection at the interop boundary.
A val property of a data class is read-only, but if its type is MutableList the collection contents can still be changed in place.
